cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: At drop-off, a father mentions that his 2-year-old woke up twice last night and skipped breakfast. What is the caregiver's most useful response?

options.a: Thank him and suggest he bring up sleep concerns at the next family conference
options.b: Watch for tiredness or hunger today and tell him at pickup how the day went
options.c: Reassure him that toddlers often skip meals and that his son will be just fine
options.d: Ask him to send a written note next time so every staff member sees the details

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Daily two-way communication means using what families share and reporting back. The caregiver uses the father's information to adjust care today (an early nap, a snack) and closes the loop at pickup, which builds trust and continuity between home and program.

distractorExplanations.a: Postpones information that matters today; a tired, hungry toddler needs adjusted care now, not weeks later.
distractorExplanations.c: Dismisses the father's report instead of acting on it and following up, which discourages him from sharing next time.
distractorExplanations.d: Puts a barrier on spoken communication; families should be able to share at drop-off and staff should pass it on.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: A grandmother who volunteers in the classroom asks the teacher why a classmate, Jayden, leaves twice a week to see a speech therapist. How should the teacher respond?

options.a: Explain briefly, since volunteers work in the room and need to understand Jayden
options.b: Share the general reason but leave out the name of Jayden's speech therapist
options.c: Politely say that information about other children's services is kept private
options.d: Suggest she ask Jayden's parents at pickup, since they may not mind sharing

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Information about a child's services, health or family is shared only with people who have a legitimate need to know and the family's permission. A volunteer's curiosity is not a need to know, so the teacher declines kindly without hinting at details.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats volunteering as permission to receive private records; volunteers do not get service details without family consent.
distractorExplanations.b: Still discloses confidential information; the general reason for therapy is as private as the therapist's name.
distractorExplanations.d: Pushes the family to explain their child's needs to a curious adult, which puts pressure on them and invites gossip.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: A teacher notices a hand-shaped bruise on a 4-year-old's upper arm. When she asks gently, the child says, "Daddy got mad." What should the teacher do next?

options.a: Ask the child more detailed questions to learn exactly what happened at home
options.b: Tell the director and let the director decide whether a report is needed
options.c: Wait a few days to see whether more bruises appear before filing a formal report
options.d: Follow policy and promptly report the suspicion to child protective services

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Child care staff are mandated reporters: reasonable suspicion is enough, and the duty to report to child protective services or the authorities is personal and prompt. The teacher also informs the director per policy and records what she saw and heard, but does not investigate or confront.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns the teacher into an investigator; repeated questioning can upset the child and taint a later forensic interview.
distractorExplanations.b: Hands off a personal legal duty; telling the director does not replace the teacher's own report when policy and law require it.
distractorExplanations.c: Waits for proof the law does not require; reasonable suspicion triggers the report, and delay can leave the child at risk.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: A teacher is preparing for a fall conference with the parents of a 3-year-old who has been biting classmates. Which plan best fits recommended practice?

options.a: Start with the child's strengths, share dated notes, and set goals together
options.b: Open with the biting incidents so the most urgent concern gets the most time
options.c: Hand the parents a written behavior plan the staff has already agreed on
options.d: Cover general milestones and save the biting concern for a later phone call

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Effective conferences start with the child's strengths, use specific, dated observations instead of general impressions, and invite the family to help set shared goals. Parents who feel their child is valued are more open to working on a concern like biting.

distractorExplanations.b: Leading with problems puts parents on the defensive; strengths first builds the trust needed to tackle the biting together.
distractorExplanations.c: Presents a finished plan instead of a partnership; families know their child and should help shape the goals.
distractorExplanations.d: Avoids the real concern the conference is meant to address, leaving the family uninformed and the biting unresolved.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: At pickup, a mother tells the teacher angrily that her son keeps coming home with paint on his clothes and "this has to stop." Other families are nearby. What is the best first response?

options.a: Explain that messy art is good for development and the program will keep it
options.b: Acknowledge her frustration and offer to talk privately about solutions
options.c: Apologize and promise to keep her son out of painting activities from now on
options.d: Send her to the director, since complaints about activities go to administration

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: A professional response to a complaint starts by listening and acknowledging the parent's feelings, then moving the conversation to a private setting to problem-solve together (smocks, a spare outfit, washable paint). This keeps the partnership intact without giving up good practice.

distractorExplanations.a: Defends the program before hearing the parent out; even a sound rationale lands badly when it dismisses her concern.
distractorExplanations.c: Gives up a valuable learning experience to end the conflict, when simple fixes could meet both needs.
distractorExplanations.d: Passes off a concern the teacher can address directly; quick referral can feel like a brush-off and delay a solution.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: A mother asks the infant teacher to rock her 7-month-old to sleep and lay him on his stomach in the crib, as she does at home. What should the teacher do?

options.a: Explain that the program uses one nap routine for every baby and cannot rock infants
options.b: Follow both requests, since the family knows the baby's sleep habits best
options.c: Rock him as she asks, then place him on his back in the crib per safe-sleep rules
options.d: Agree to the stomach position as long as the mother signs a written permission note

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Programs honor family routines whenever they are safe, so rocking to sleep can be continued. Safe-sleep standards require placing infants on their backs in the crib to reduce SIDS risk; a different position needs a physician's written instruction, not a parent request.

distractorExplanations.a: Rejects a safe family practice for the sake of uniformity; individualized routines help infants feel secure.
distractorExplanations.b: Respects the family but breaks back-to-sleep rules, which exist because stomach sleeping raises SIDS risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a parent note as enough; departing from back-sleeping requires a physician's written medical instruction.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: A woman staff have seen at family events arrives to pick up 3-year-old Mia. She says she is Mia's aunt, but she is not on the authorized pickup list. What should the caregiver do?

options.a: Release Mia, since Mia knows her and staff have seen her with the family before
options.b: Release Mia once the aunt shows a photo ID and signs the sign-out sheet
options.c: Release Mia if the aunt can show a text from the parent asking her to come
options.d: Keep Mia in care, call a parent, and follow policy for adding a pickup adult

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Children are released to adults the parent has authorized in writing, and staff check ID against that list. When someone unlisted arrives, the child stays in care while staff contact the parent and follow the program's written procedure for adding a new pickup person.

distractorExplanations.a: Relies on familiarity instead of authorization; a known relative may still be barred by a custody order.
distractorExplanations.b: Checks identity but not permission; ID proves who she is, not that the parent authorized her.
distractorExplanations.c: Accepts a text that staff cannot verify; it could be forged or sent from someone else's phone.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: During circle time, a co-teacher tells the children they will lose outdoor play if they keep talking. The lead teacher disagrees with this approach. What should the lead teacher do?

options.a: Talk with the co-teacher privately later and agree on a shared approach
options.b: Correct the co-teacher right away so the children see the threat is withdrawn
options.c: Report the co-teacher to the director before talking with her directly about it
options.d: Let it go to keep the peace, since each teacher has a personal style

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Staff disagreements are handled respectfully and away from children, then resolved into a consistent approach. Talking with the co-teacher directly first follows the NAEYC Code's guidance on working with colleagues and gives children predictable guidance from both adults.

distractorExplanations.b: Undermines a colleague in front of the children, which confuses them and damages the teaching partnership.
distractorExplanations.c: Skips the colleague-to-colleague step; for a practice concern that is not harmful, talk directly before escalating.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaves an ineffective practice in place; teaching teams need a shared, consistent guidance approach.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: Over two weeks, a teacher's notes show that 4-year-old Sam spends most free-choice time building ramps and rolling cars down them. What is the best use of these observations?

options.a: Steer Sam to the art area more often so he tries a wider range of activities
options.b: Add ramp pieces and balls of different sizes to extend his experiments
options.c: File the notes in his portfolio and review them for the end-of-year report
options.d: Show the notes to his family as proof that he is ahead in science skills

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Observations are most valuable when they guide planning. Sam's sustained interest in ramps is a chance to deepen his learning about slope, speed and cause and effect by adding materials that invite new experiments and questions.

distractorExplanations.a: Pulls Sam away from a strong interest instead of building on it; interest-based learning keeps children engaged.
distractorExplanations.c: Stores observations without using them; notes should shape planning now, not wait months for a report.
distractorExplanations.d: Turns a play observation into a label; two weeks of ramp play does not show he is ahead of peers.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: After a fun field trip, an assistant teacher wants to post a photo of the class on her personal social media account. What does professional ethics require?

options.a: She may post it if she leaves out the children's names and the center's name
options.b: She may post it if her account is private and limited to close friends and family
options.c: Use program channels that follow family photo permissions, not her own account
options.d: She may post it if most families have said they enjoy seeing class photos

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Children's images are confidential information. Photos are shared only through program channels and only for children whose families gave written permission. Posting on a personal account takes control of the images away from families, even without names.

distractorExplanations.a: A face is identifying on its own; removing names does not replace written family permission.
distractorExplanations.b: Private settings do not make it ethical; friends can share or screenshot the photo, and families did not consent.
distractorExplanations.d: Majority approval is not consent; each family decides about its own child, and some may have safety reasons to refuse.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: For two months, a teacher has observed that a 20-month-old rarely babbles, seldom responds to his name, and uses no words. How should she share this with the family?

options.a: Tell the parents the signs suggest autism so they can seek treatment quickly
options.b: Suggest waiting until he turns 3, since many children start talking late
options.c: Refer the family to the public school district for a special education evaluation
options.d: Describe what she has seen and share how to contact early intervention

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Caregivers describe what they have seen, not a diagnosis. For a child under 3, the referral path is the state's Part C early intervention program, which offers a free evaluation; the public school district handles evaluations from age 3. Early referral matters because services work best when started early.

distractorExplanations.a: Offers a diagnosis the caregiver is not qualified to make; describe observations and let specialists evaluate.
distractorExplanations.b: Delays help during a key window; possible signs at 20 months call for referral now, not a wait-and-see plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses the wrong system for his age; school districts evaluate from age 3, while under-3s go to Part C early intervention.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: At drop-off, a parent tells the teacher that the family has moved and has new emergency contact phone numbers. What should the teacher do?

options.a: Update the emergency file right away and tell the child's caregivers
options.b: Make a note to update the records at the next scheduled file review
options.c: Save the new numbers on her phone so she can reach the family if needed
options.d: Ask the parent to bring the updated details to the next family conference

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Emergency contact and health records must be current and accessible to every adult caring for the child, including substitutes and staff on field trips. An outdated record can delay reaching a family in an injury, illness or evacuation, so changes are recorded right away.

distractorExplanations.b: Leaves wrong numbers in the file until the review; an emergency could happen before then.
distractorExplanations.c: Keeps the information where other staff cannot reach it and stores family data on a personal device.
distractorExplanations.d: Delays a simple, urgent update; emergency information does not wait for a conference.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: A teacher is writing anecdotal notes during center time. Which entry is the best example of an objective anecdotal record?

options.a: Leo was angry and aggressive in the block area because he did not want to share.
options.b: 10:15, blocks: Leo pushed over Ana's tower, said "Mine!" and walked away.
options.c: Leo had another bad morning and seems to struggle with sharing toys in general.
options.d: Leo is showing signs of an attention problem during center time in the blocks.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: An objective anecdotal record states the time, place and exactly what the child did and said, like a camera would capture it. Interpretations, feelings and labels are left out of the record so that the notes can be used fairly for planning and family conversations.

distractorExplanations.a: Adds interpretation ("angry," "aggressive," "did not want to share") that the observer cannot actually see.
distractorExplanations.c: Gives an opinion and a generalization ("another bad morning") instead of describing one specific event.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies a clinical label; teachers record behavior and leave any diagnosis to qualified professionals.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: A preschool teacher is planning next month's curriculum for a group of 4- and 5-year-olds. Which approach best reflects developmentally appropriate program planning?

options.a: Follow a set worksheet sequence so each child covers the same letters weekly
options.b: Plan around a kindergarten readiness checklist and drill the skills children lack
options.c: Build on children's observed interests with hands-on activities across domains
options.d: Let children choose freely through the day without teacher-planned goals

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Developmentally appropriate planning for 4- and 5-year-olds uses observations of children's interests and abilities to design hands-on, play-based experiences that support social, emotional, physical, language and cognitive growth together, with clear teacher goals behind them.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores individual differences and relies on worksheets, which are a poor fit for how preschoolers learn.
distractorExplanations.b: Narrows the curriculum to drilled skills and overlooks social-emotional growth and play-based learning.
distractorExplanations.d: Removes intentional teaching; free choice works best when teachers plan the materials and goals behind it.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.prompt: After a group time where several children wandered away, a teacher wants to improve her practice. Which step best shows reflective practice?

options.a: Decide the group is too young for circle time and drop it from the schedule
options.b: Ask the director for a firmer rule about staying seated during group time
options.c: Sign up for the next available workshop on general classroom management
options.d: Review what happened, ask why interest faded, and adjust the plan

cda-childcare-readiness-check-families-p.explanation: Reflective practice means looking honestly at one's own teaching: what happened, why, and what to change. Examining length, content and timing of group time leads to a targeted adjustment, and the cycle continues with the next observation.

distractorExplanations.a: Reacts to one hard day by removing a valuable routine instead of analyzing what made it hard to follow.
distractorExplanations.b: Looks for a stricter rule instead of examining the teaching; the children's interest is the real issue.
distractorExplanations.c: Training can help, but a generic workshop skips examining what went wrong in this specific group time.
